newsitem.title: UK: Sterling steady as budget vigil enters final hours.
newsitem.headline: Sterling steady as budget vigil enters final hours.

text.p: Sterling was little changed in morning European trade, with traders expected to take their cue from the severity with which UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown clamps down on the consumer in his budget later on Wednesday.

Mounting evidence of the strength of domestic demand have stoked expectations of higher UK interest rates and boosted sterling almost 2 percent in the past week against the mark to its highest levels in five years.
The pound's outlook now depends on whether the budget leaves the Bank of England's monetary policy committee to bear the brunt of fighting inflation, analysts said.

"There is a suspicion that Brown will hit the consumer and take the pressure off monetary policy," said Ian Morris, international economist at HSBC James Capel. "Sterling will weaken if this is the case, but if it is not, it will rally with the potential to hit three (per mark) eventually."
The pound was at 2.8980/90 marks at 0925 GMT against 2.8875/85 late Tuesday in Europe. Cable was at $1.6588/98 against $1.6575/80 yesterday.
Economists are expecting Brown to use Labour's first budget in almost two decades to tighten fiscal policy by about four billion pounds.
The key for currency traders is how much of this tightening comes at the expense of the British consumer who has been fuelling growth in recent quarters.
UK rates are at 6.5 percent having risen in two quarter-percentage point jumps since the Labour government came to power on May 1. The increases have yet to dent domestic demand.

Most recent data showed retail sales are rising at their strongest levels since the late 1980s, with UK consumers borrowing more than one billion pounds in May. The housing market has also proved resilient, with the Nationwide reporting an 11.0 percent increase in house prices in the year to June.

"The net fiscal tightening is important but how much the consumer and the housing market gets hit is what sterling will be looking for since that is what will affect base rate expectations," said Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN Amro.
Labour's election promises will limit Brown's ability to curb consumption. Hopes of higher rates should therefore persist whatever measures are included in the budget, analysts said.
Still, sterling's pullback from recent highs risks turning into a more extended slump if the budget spurs traders to scale back expectations of how high rates will rise in this economic cycle.

Short sterling futures contracts indicate that rates are expected to peak late next year. September 1998 short sterling is at 92.69, implying rates of 7.31 percent by the end of the third quarter next year. -Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
